questions.question: In C runtime environment, which one of the following is stored in heap?

options.A: A static variable declared inside a function
options.B: An array of integers declared inside a function
options.C: A dynamically allocated array of integers created using malloc() function call

questions.explanation: In the C runtime memory model: - A static variable declared inside a function is stored in the data/BSS segment (its lifetime spans the whole program), not the heap. - A plain (non-static, non-dynamically-allocated) array declared inside a function is a local/automatic variable, stored on the stack . - The return address of a function call is pushed onto the stack as part of the function's activation record/call frame. - Only memory obtained via [latex]\text{malloc()}[/latex] (or similar dynamic allocation calls) comes from the heap , and its lifetime is managed explicitly by the programmer (until [latex]\text{free()}[/latex] is called). Answer: A dynamically allocated array of integers created using malloc() Click here for detail solution
questions.explanation_html:
In the C runtime memory model:

- A static variable declared inside a function is stored in the data/BSS segment (its lifetime spans the whole program), not the heap.
- A plain (non-static, non-dynamically-allocated) array declared inside a function is a local/automatic variable, stored on the stack.
- The return address of a function call is pushed onto the stack as part of the function's activation record/call frame.
- Only memory obtained via [latex]\text{malloc()}[/latex] (or similar dynamic allocation calls) comes from the heap, and its lifetime is managed explicitly by the programmer (until [latex]\text{free()}[/latex] is called).

Answer: A dynamically allocated array of integers created using malloc()

questions.question: Consider the following two statements about interrupt handling mechanisms in a CPU. [latex]\text{S1}[/latex]: In non-vectored interrupt mechanism, it usually takes more time to start the Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) when compared to that in a vectored interrupt mechanism. [latex]\text{S2}[/latex]: In daisy-chain interrupt mechanism, the CPU polls all the input devices individually to determine the source of the interrupt. Which one of the following options is correct with respect to [latex]\text{S1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{S2}?[/latex]
questions.explanation: S1: In a non-vectored interrupt scheme, the CPU typically must poll each device (or run a fixed interrupt-service routine that then figures out which device raised the interrupt) to determine the interrupt source and its ISR address, which takes extra time compared to a vectored scheme where the interrupting device directly supplies (or a lookup table directly provides) the address of its specific ISR. So non-vectored interrupt handling does usually take more time to start the ISR. S1 is true. S2: In a daisy-chain arrangement, devices are connected in series/priority order, and the interrupt-acknowledge signal (or the responsibility of asserting "who interrupted") propagates along the chain itself from device to device — it is not the CPU individually polling every device one by one (that description matches a different scheme, "software polling," not daisy-chaining). So S2 is false. Answer: S1 is true and S2 is false. Click here for detail solution
questions.explanation_html:
S1: In a non-vectored interrupt scheme, the CPU typically must poll each device (or run a fixed interrupt-service routine that then figures out which device raised the interrupt) to determine the interrupt source and its ISR address, which takes extra time compared to a vectored scheme where the interrupting device directly supplies (or a lookup table directly provides) the address of its specific ISR. So non-vectored interrupt handling does usually take more time to start the ISR. S1 is true.

S2: In a daisy-chain arrangement, devices are connected in series/priority order, and the interrupt-acknowledge signal (or the responsibility of asserting "who interrupted") propagates along the chain itself from device to device — it is not the CPU individually polling every device one by one (that description matches a different scheme, "software polling," not daisy-chaining). So S2 is false.

Answer: S1 is true and S2 is false.

questions.question: Consider concurrent execution of two transactions [latex]T 1[/latex] and [latex]T 2[/latex] in a DBMS, both of which access a data object [latex]A[/latex]. For these two transactions to not conflict on [latex]A[/latex], which one of the following statements must be true?
questions.explanation: Two operations by different transactions on the same data object [latex]A[/latex] "conflict" (in the standard DBMS concurrency-control sense) precisely when at least one of them is a write — i.e. any of read-write, write-read, or write-write pairs are conflicting, because the order in which they execute can change the outcome. The only combination that never conflicts is when both transactions merely read [latex]A[/latex] — reads never interfere with each other regardless of execution order, since neither changes the value of [latex]A[/latex]. Answer: Both T1 and T2 only read A. Click here for detail solution

The only combination that never conflicts is when both transactions merely read [latex]A[/latex] — reads never interfere with each other regardless of execution order, since neither changes the value of [latex]A[/latex].

Answer: Both T1 and T2 only read A.

questions.question: Which one of the following protocols may need to broadcast some of its messages?
questions.explanation: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) is used by a host to automatically obtain an IP address (and other network configuration) when it first joins a network — since the host doesn't yet have an IP address (or know the server's address), its initial "DHCP Discover" message must be broadcast on the local network so that any DHCP server present can respond. [latex]\text{SMTP}[/latex] (mail), [latex]\text{FTP}[/latex] (file transfer), and [latex]\text{HTTP}[/latex] (web) are all conventional client-server protocols that communicate with a specific, already-known server address over a normal unicast connection — they have no inherent need to broadcast. Answer: DHCP Click here for detail solution

questions.question: Which one of the following CPU scheduling algorithms cannot be preemptive?
questions.explanation: Checking whether each scheduling algorithm supports preemption: - SRTF is explicitly the preemptive version of Shortest-Job-First — it can preempt a running process whenever a newly arrived process has a shorter remaining time. - Round Robin is inherently preemptive — it forcibly preempts a running process once its time quantum expires. - Priority Scheduling can be implemented in either a preemptive form (a higher-priority arrival preempts the current process) or non-preemptive form — so it certainly can be preemptive. - FCFS (First Come First Serve) is defined by running processes strictly to completion in arrival order — there is no mechanism within FCFS for a later-arriving process to interrupt/preempt the one currently executing. It is inherently non-preemptive by definition. Answer: First Come First Serve (FCFS) Scheduling cannot be preemptive. Click here for detail solution
questions.explanation_html:
Checking whether each scheduling algorithm supports preemption:

- SRTF is explicitly the preemptive version of Shortest-Job-First — it can preempt a running process whenever a newly arrived process has a shorter remaining time.
- Round Robin is inherently preemptive — it forcibly preempts a running process once its time quantum expires.
- Priority Scheduling can be implemented in either a preemptive form (a higher-priority arrival preempts the current process) or non-preemptive form — so it certainly can be preemptive.
- FCFS (First Come First Serve) is defined by running processes strictly to completion in arrival order — there is no mechanism within FCFS for a later-arriving process to interrupt/preempt the one currently executing. It is inherently non-preemptive by definition.

Answer: First Come First Serve (FCFS) Scheduling cannot be preemptive.

questions.question: Consider the following functions, where [latex]n[/latex] is a positive integer. [latex] n^{1 / 3}, \log (n), \log (n!), 2^{\log (n)} [/latex] Which one of the following options lists the functions in increasing order of asymptotic growth rate? Note: Assume the base of log to be [latex]2[/latex].
questions.explanation: Simplify each function's asymptotic growth (using [latex]\log[/latex] base [latex]2[/latex]): - [latex]\log(n)[/latex]: grows the slowest of all — sub-polynomial. - [latex]n^{1/3}[/latex]: a polynomial with a small (fractional) exponent, grows faster than any power of [latex]\log n[/latex] but slower than [latex]n[/latex] itself. - [latex]2^{\log(n)}=n[/latex] (since exponentiating base [latex]2[/latex] by [latex]\log_2 n[/latex] simply recovers [latex]n[/latex]) — so this grows exactly like [latex]n[/latex], faster than [latex]n^{1/3}[/latex]. - [latex]\log(n!)[/latex]: by Stirling's approximation, [latex]\log(n!)=\Theta(n\log n)[/latex], which grows faster than plain [latex]n[/latex] (and hence faster than [latex]2^{\log n}=n[/latex]). So the increasing order is: [latex]\log(n) \;<\; n^{1/3} \;<\; 2^{\log(n)} \;<\; \log(n!)[/latex]. Answer: log(n), n^(1/3), 2^log(n), log(n!) Click here for detail solution
questions.explanation_html:
Simplify each function's asymptotic growth (using [latex]\log[/latex] base [latex]2[/latex]):

- [latex]\log(n)[/latex]: grows the slowest of all — sub-polynomial.
- [latex]n^{1/3}[/latex]: a polynomial with a small (fractional) exponent, grows faster than any power of [latex]\log n[/latex] but slower than [latex]n[/latex] itself.
- [latex]2^{\log(n)}=n[/latex] (since exponentiating base [latex]2[/latex] by [latex]\log_2 n[/latex] simply recovers [latex]n[/latex]) — so this grows exactly like [latex]n[/latex], faster than [latex]n^{1/3}[/latex].
- [latex]\log(n!)[/latex]: by Stirling's approximation, [latex]\log(n!)=\Theta(n\log n)[/latex], which grows faster than plain [latex]n[/latex] (and hence faster than [latex]2^{\log n}=n[/latex]).

So the increasing order is: [latex]\log(n) \;<\; n^{1/3} \;<\; 2^{\log(n)} \;<\; \log(n!)[/latex].

Answer: log(n), n^(1/3), 2^log(n), log(n!)

questions.question: Which of the following can be recurrence relation(s) corresponding to an algorithm with time complexity [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]?
questions.explanation: Solve each recurrence and compare to [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]: - [latex]T(n)=T(n-1)+1[/latex]: unrolling gives [latex]T(n)=T(1)+(n-1)\times1=\Theta(n)[/latex]. Matches. - [latex]T(n)=2T(n/2)+1[/latex]: by the Master theorem, [latex]a=2,b=2[/latex] so [latex]n^{\log_2 2}=n^1=n[/latex]; since [latex]f(n)=1[/latex] is polynomially smaller than [latex]n[/latex], Case 1 gives [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n)[/latex]. Matches. - [latex]T(n)=2T(n/2)+n[/latex]: this is the classic merge-sort recurrence, [latex]f(n)=n=n^{\log_2 2}[/latex] exactly (Case 2), giving [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n\log n)[/latex] — not [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]. - [latex]T(n)=T(n-1)+n[/latex]: unrolling gives [latex]T(n)=\Theta(1+2+\cdots+n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex] — not [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]. Answer: T(n)=T(n-1)+1 and T(n)=2T(n/2)+1 both correspond to Θ(n) algorithms. Click here for detail solution

Solve each recurrence and compare to [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]:

- [latex]T(n)=T(n-1)+1[/latex]: unrolling gives [latex]T(n)=T(1)+(n-1)\times1=\Theta(n)[/latex]. Matches.
- [latex]T(n)=2T(n/2)+1[/latex]: by the Master theorem, [latex]a=2,b=2[/latex] so [latex]n^{\log_2 2}=n^1=n[/latex]; since [latex]f(n)=1[/latex] is polynomially smaller than [latex]n[/latex], Case 1 gives [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n)[/latex]. Matches.
- [latex]T(n)=2T(n/2)+n[/latex]: this is the classic merge-sort recurrence, [latex]f(n)=n=n^{\log_2 2}[/latex] exactly (Case 2), giving [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n\log n)[/latex] — not [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].
- [latex]T(n)=T(n-1)+n[/latex]: unrolling gives [latex]T(n)=\Theta(1+2+\cdots+n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex] — not [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].

Answer: T(n)=T(n-1)+1 and T(n)=2T(n/2)+1 both correspond to Θ(n) algorithms.

questions.question: Let [latex]R[/latex] be a binary relation on the set [latex]\{1,2, \ldots, 10\}[/latex], where [latex](x, y) \in R[/latex] if the product of [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] is square of an integer. Which of the following properties is/are satisfied by [latex]R[/latex]?
questions.explanation: [latex](x,y)\in R[/latex] iff [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square. - Reflexive: [latex]x\cdot x=x^2[/latex] is always a perfect square, so [latex](x,x)\in R[/latex] for every [latex]x[/latex]. Holds. - Symmetric: [latex]xy=yx[/latex], so if [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square then so is [latex]yx[/latex] (the same number). Holds. - Transitive: Write each number as [latex]n=k^2\cdot s[/latex] where [latex]s[/latex] is its square-free part. Then [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square exactly when [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] have the same square-free part. This "same square-free part" relation is a genuine equivalence relation, so it is transitive: if [latex]x,y[/latex] share a square-free part and [latex]y,z[/latex] share the same square-free part, then [latex]x,z[/latex] do too, making [latex]xz[/latex] a perfect square. Holds. - Antisymmetric: a counterexample: [latex]x=2,y=8[/latex] gives [latex]xy=16=4^2[/latex], so [latex](2,8)\in R[/latex] and (by symmetry) [latex](8,2)\in R[/latex] too, even though [latex]2\ne8[/latex]. Fails. Answer: Reflexive, Symmetric, and Transitive all hold (R is an equivalence relation); Antisymmetric does not hold. Click here for detail solution

[latex](x,y)\in R[/latex] iff [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square.

- Reflexive: [latex]x\cdot x=x^2[/latex] is always a perfect square, so [latex](x,x)\in R[/latex] for every [latex]x[/latex]. Holds.
- Symmetric: [latex]xy=yx[/latex], so if [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square then so is [latex]yx[/latex] (the same number). Holds.
- Transitive: Write each number as [latex]n=k^2\cdot s[/latex] where [latex]s[/latex] is its square-free part. Then [latex]xy[/latex] is a perfect square exactly when [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] have the same square-free part. This "same square-free part" relation is a genuine equivalence relation, so it is transitive: if [latex]x,y[/latex] share a square-free part and [latex]y,z[/latex] share the same square-free part, then [latex]x,z[/latex] do too, making [latex]xz[/latex] a perfect square. Holds.
- Antisymmetric: a counterexample: [latex]x=2,y=8[/latex] gives [latex]xy=16=4^2[/latex], so [latex](2,8)\in R[/latex] and (by symmetry) [latex](8,2)\in R[/latex] too, even though [latex]2\ne8[/latex]. Fails.

questions.question: For a real number [latex]a[/latex], let [latex]I(a)=\int_{-1}^{1}\left(3 x^{2}-a x+1\right) d x[/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.A: The value of [latex]I(a)[/latex] is independent of the value of [latex]a[/latex]
options.B: The value of [latex]I(a)[/latex] can vary with the value of [latex]a[/latex]
options.C: There exists [latex]a \in(-\infty,+\infty)[/latex] such that [latex]I(a)[/latex] is a positive real number
options.D: There exists [latex]a \in(-\infty,+\infty)[/latex] such that [latex]I(a)[/latex] is a negative real number

questions.explanation: [latex]I(a)=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}(3x^2-ax+1)\,dx[/latex] The middle term [latex]-ax[/latex] is an odd function of [latex]x[/latex], so its integral over the symmetric interval [latex][-1,1][/latex] is exactly [latex]0[/latex], regardless of the value of [latex]a[/latex]. Only the even part survives: [latex]I(a)=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^1(3x^2+1)\,dx=\Big[x^3+x\Big]_{-1}^{1}=(1+1)-(-1-1)=2-(-2)=4[/latex] So [latex]I(a)=4[/latex] for every real [latex]a[/latex] — the value is completely independent of [latex]a[/latex]. Since it's always [latex]4>0[/latex], there certainly exists (in fact, every) [latex]a[/latex] for which [latex]I(a)[/latex] is a positive real number; but there is no [latex]a[/latex] making it negative, and the value does not "vary." Answer: I(a) is independent of a; and there exists a for which I(a) is positive (true for every a, since I(a)=4 always). Click here for detail solution
questions.explanation_html:
[latex]I(a)=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}(3x^2-ax+1)\,dx[/latex]

The middle term [latex]-ax[/latex] is an odd function of [latex]x[/latex], so its integral over the symmetric interval [latex][-1,1][/latex] is exactly [latex]0[/latex], regardless of the value of [latex]a[/latex]. Only the even part survives:
[latex]I(a)=\displaystyle\int_{-1}^1(3x^2+1)\,dx=\Big[x^3+x\Big]_{-1}^{1}=(1+1)-(-1-1)=2-(-2)=4[/latex]

So [latex]I(a)=4[/latex] for every real [latex]a[/latex] — the value is completely independent of [latex]a[/latex]. Since it's always [latex]4>0[/latex], there certainly exists (in fact, every) [latex]a[/latex] for which [latex]I(a)[/latex] is a positive real number; but there is no [latex]a[/latex] making it negative, and the value does not "vary."

Answer: I(a) is independent of a; and there exists a for which I(a) is positive (true for every a, since I(a)=4 always).

questions.question: Which of the following grammars is/are ambiguous?
questions.explanation: Checking each grammar for ambiguity (does some string have two distinct parse trees?): - [latex]S\rightarrow aSb\mid\epsilon[/latex]: generates only [latex]a^nb^n[/latex], with a unique nested derivation for every string — unambiguous . - [latex]E\rightarrow E+E\mid E*E\mid id[/latex]: the classic textbook example of an ambiguous grammar — e.g. [latex]id+id*id[/latex] can be parsed with two different groupings (no precedence/associativity is encoded), giving two distinct parse trees. - [latex]S\rightarrow aS\mid Sa\mid\epsilon[/latex]: generates strings of [latex]a[/latex]'s only, but because both left-recursion ([latex]Sa[/latex]) and right-recursion ([latex]aS[/latex]) are available, a string like "[latex]aa[/latex]" can be built in more than one structurally distinct way — ambiguous . - [latex]S\rightarrow aS\mid\epsilon[/latex]: purely right-recursive, unique derivation for every string — unambiguous . Answer: [latex]E\rightarrow E+E|E*E|id[/latex] and [latex]S\rightarrow aS|Sa|\epsilon[/latex] are ambiguous. Click here for detail solution

questions.question: Consider the system of linear equations given below. [latex] \begin{array}{c} a x+y=b \\ 16 x+a y=24 \end{array} [/latex] Suppose the values of [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] are chosen such that the system of linear equations produce multiple solutions. Then the product of [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] is ________. (answer in integer)
questions.explanation: The system [latex]ax+y=b,\ 16x+ay=24[/latex] has infinitely many (multiple) solutions exactly when the two equations describe the same line , i.e. all three coefficient ratios are equal: [latex]\dfrac{a}{16}=\dfrac{1}{a}=\dfrac{b}{24}[/latex] From [latex]\dfrac{a}{16}=\dfrac{1}{a}[/latex]: [latex]a^2=16\Rightarrow a=\pm4[/latex]. From [latex]\dfrac{1}{a}=\dfrac{b}{24}[/latex]: [latex]b=\dfrac{24}{a}[/latex]. If [latex]a=4[/latex]: [latex]b=24/4=6[/latex], so [latex]ab=4\times6=24[/latex]. If [latex]a=-4[/latex]: [latex]b=24/(-4)=-6[/latex], so [latex]ab=(-4)\times(-6)=24[/latex]. Either valid choice of [latex]a[/latex] gives the same product. Answer: 24 Click here for detail solution
questions.explanation_html:
The system [latex]ax+y=b,\ 16x+ay=24[/latex] has infinitely many (multiple) solutions exactly when the two equations describe the same line, i.e. all three coefficient ratios are equal:
[latex]\dfrac{a}{16}=\dfrac{1}{a}=\dfrac{b}{24}[/latex]

From [latex]\dfrac{a}{16}=\dfrac{1}{a}[/latex]: [latex]a^2=16\Rightarrow a=\pm4[/latex].
From [latex]\dfrac{1}{a}=\dfrac{b}{24}[/latex]: [latex]b=\dfrac{24}{a}[/latex].

If [latex]a=4[/latex]: [latex]b=24/4=6[/latex], so [latex]ab=4\times6=24[/latex].
If [latex]a=-4[/latex]: [latex]b=24/(-4)=-6[/latex], so [latex]ab=(-4)\times(-6)=24[/latex].

Either valid choice of [latex]a[/latex] gives the same product.

Answer: 24

questions.question: Consider an array [latex]A=[10,7,8,19,41,35,25,31][/latex]. Suppose the merge sort algorithm is executed on array [latex]A[/latex] to sort it in increasing order. A merge operation on sorted left array [latex]L[/latex] and sorted right array [latex]R[/latex] is said to be void if the output of the merge operation is the elements of array [latex]L[/latex] followed by the elements of array [latex]R[/latex]. The number of void merge operations among these [latex]7[/latex] merge operations is ________. (answer in integer)
questions.explanation: A merge is void when every element of the left sub-array is already [latex]\le[/latex] every element of the right sub-array, so the merge simply concatenates them with no interleaving. [latex][8],[19]\to[8,19][/latex] (already [latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex] as-is) — void . [latex][41],[35]\to[35,41][/latex] — not void . [latex][25],[31]\to[25,31][/latex] (already in order) — void . Next level (quads): [latex][7,10]+[8,19]\to[7,8,10,19][/latex] (interleaved, not simply [latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex]) — not void . [latex][35,41]+[25,31]\to[25,31,35,41][/latex] (interleaved) — not void . Final merge: [latex][7,8,10,19]+[25,31,35,41][/latex]: every element of the left ([latex]\le19[/latex]) is already smaller than every element of the right ([latex]\ge25[/latex]), so the merge is simply [latex]L[/latex] followed by [latex]R[/latex] — void . Total merges [latex]=4+2+1=7[/latex] (matches the given count), with exactly [latex]3[/latex] of them void. Answer: 3 Click here for detail solution
questions.explanation_html:
A merge is void when every element of the left sub-array is already [latex]\le[/latex] every element of the right sub-array, so the merge simply concatenates them with no interleaving.

Note that multiple spanning trees can be constructed over [latex]K_{n}[/latex]. Each of these spanning trees is represented as a set of edges. The Jaccard coefficient between any two sets is defined as the ratio of the size of the intersection of the two sets to the size of the union of the two sets. Which one of the following options gives the lowest possible value for the Jaccard coefficient between any two spanning trees of [latex]K_{n}[/latex] ?
questions.explanation: The Jaccard coefficient between two spanning-tree edge sets is [latex]\dfrac{|E_1\cap E_2|}{|E_1\cup E_2|}[/latex], which reaches its lowest possible value [latex]0[/latex] precisely when the two spanning trees share no edges at all (completely edge-disjoint spanning trees). In [latex]K_n[/latex] for [latex]n>4[/latex], there are more than enough edges ([latex]\binom{n}{2}[/latex] total, versus only [latex]n-1[/latex] needed per spanning tree) to always construct two entirely edge-disjoint spanning trees (this is guaranteed by well-known results on edge-disjoint spanning trees in dense graphs, e.g. via Nash-Williams/Tutte-style constructions). When the intersection is empty, the Jaccard coefficient is exactly [latex]0[/latex], which is also the theoretical minimum possible value for any Jaccard coefficient. Answer: 0 Click here for detail solution

questions.question: Let [latex]G[/latex] be a weighted directed acyclic graph with [latex]m[/latex] edges and [latex]n[/latex] vertices. Given [latex]G[/latex] and a source vertex [latex]s[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex], which one of the following options gives the worst case time complexity of the fastest algorithm to find the lengths of shortest paths from [latex]s[/latex] to all vertices that are reachable from [latex]s[/latex] in [latex]{G}?[/latex]
questions.explanation: For a directed acyclic graph (DAG) , the fastest known algorithm for single-source shortest paths uses the following two steps: (1) compute a topological ordering of the vertices in [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex] time, then (2) process vertices in that topological order, relaxing every outgoing edge of each vertex exactly once, which takes [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex] time in total (this correctly computes shortest paths since, in topological order, all edges into a vertex are relaxed before that vertex is finalized, and no negative cycles can exist in a DAG so ordinary Dijkstra-style priority queues or Bellman-Ford repeated relaxation are unnecessary). This is strictly faster than Dijkstra's [latex]\Theta(m+n\log n)[/latex] (needed only for general graphs with a priority queue) or the [latex]\Theta(nm)[/latex] Bellman-Ford bound (needed for general graphs, possibly with negative edges but no negative cycles) — the DAG structure lets us avoid both. Answer: [latex]\Theta(m+n)[/latex] Click here for detail solution

questions.question: Consider an array [latex]A[/latex] of integers of size [latex]n[/latex]. The indices of [latex]A[/latex] run from [latex]1[/latex] to [latex]n[/latex]. questions.explanation: The condition says: for every pair of indices [latex]i>j[/latex] (both in [latex]\{1,\ldots,n-1\}[/latex]), the consecutive difference [latex]D[i]=A[i+1]-A[i][/latex] must exceed [latex]D[j]=A[j+1]-A[j][/latex]. In other words, the sequence of consecutive differences [latex]D[1],D[2],\ldots,D[n-1][/latex] must be strictly increasing (array [latex]A[/latex] is "convex"). This can be checked with a single linear pass: compute each [latex]D[i]=A[i+1]-A[i][/latex] and verify [latex]D[i]>D[i-1][/latex] for each consecutive pair, stopping early with "no" the first time this fails. This takes [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] time, and it's optimal since every element of the array must be examined at least once to certify the condition holds. Answer: [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] Click here for detail solution

questions.question: Consider the canonical [latex]L R(0)[/latex] parsing of the grammar below using terminals [latex]\{a, b, c\}[/latex] and non-terminals [latex]\{A, B, C, S\}[/latex] with [latex]S[/latex] as the start symbol. [latex] \begin{array}{l} S \rightarrow A C B \\ A \rightarrow a A \mid \epsilon \\ C \rightarrow c C \mid \epsilon \\ B \rightarrow b B \mid b \end{array} [/latex] Which one of the following options gives the number of shift-reduce conflicts that will occur in the [latex]L R(0)[/latex] ACTION table?
questions.explanation: Building the LR(0) canonical collection for [latex]S\to ACB,\ A\to aA|\epsilon,\ C\to cC|\epsilon,\ B\to bB|b[/latex], a state has a shift-reduce conflict whenever it contains both a complete (reduce) item and a shift item on some terminal. Tracing through the automaton, the following states each mix a reduce item with a shift item: - The initial state [latex]\{S'\to\cdot S,\ S\to\cdot ACB,\ A\to\cdot aA,\ A\to\cdot\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]A\to\epsilon[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]a[/latex]. - The state reached after [latex]A[/latex], [latex]\{S\to A\cdot CB,\ C\to\cdot cC,\ C\to\cdot\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]C\to\epsilon[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]c[/latex]. - The self-looping state on [latex]a[/latex], [latex]\{A\to a\cdot A,\ A\to\cdot aA,\ A\to\cdot\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]A\to\epsilon[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]a[/latex]. - The self-looping state on [latex]c[/latex], [latex]\{C\to c\cdot C,\ C\to\cdot cC,\ C\to\cdot\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]C\to\epsilon[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]c[/latex]. - The self-looping state on [latex]b[/latex] (from [latex]B\to bB|b[/latex]), [latex]\{B\to b\cdot B,\ B\to b\cdot,\ B\to\cdot bB,\ B\to\cdot b\}[/latex]: reduce [latex]B\to b[/latex] vs. shift on [latex]b[/latex]. That gives exactly [latex]5[/latex] conflicting states (all other states, such as the ones after fully reducing [latex]A,C,B,[/latex] or [latex]S[/latex], contain only a single complete item and no competing shift). questions.question: In the context of schema normalization in relational DBMS, consider a set [latex]\text{F}[/latex] of functional dependencies. The set of all functional dependencies implied by [latex]\text{F}[/latex] is called the closure of [latex]\text{F}[/latex]. To compute the closure of [latex]\text{F}[/latex], Armstrong's Axioms can be applied. Consider [latex]X, Y[/latex], and [latex]Z[/latex] as sets of attributes over a relational schema. The three rules of Armstrong's Axioms are described as follows. Reflexivity: If [latex]Y \subseteq X[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] Augmentation: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex], then [latex]X Z \rightarrow Y Z[/latex] for any Z Transitivity: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] and [latex]Y \rightarrow Z[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Z[/latex] The additional rule of Union is defined as follows. Union: If [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] and [latex]X \rightarrow Z[/latex], then [latex]X \rightarrow Y Z[/latex] It can be proved that the additional rule of Union is also implied by the three rules of Armstrong's Axioms. Listed below are four combinations of these three rules. Which one of these combinations is both necessary and sufficient for the proof?
questions.explanation: The standard proof of the Union rule ([latex]X\to Y,\,X\to Z\;\Rightarrow\;X\to YZ[/latex]) proceeds as follows: 1. [latex]X\to Y[/latex] (given). By Augmentation (adding [latex]X[/latex] to both sides): [latex]X\to XY[/latex] (using [latex]XX=X[/latex]). 2. [latex]X\to Z[/latex] (given). By Augmentation (adding [latex]Y[/latex] to both sides): [latex]XY\to YZ[/latex]. 3. Combining steps 1 and 2 via Transitivity : [latex]X\to XY[/latex] and [latex]XY\to YZ[/latex] gives [latex]X\to YZ[/latex]. This derivation only ever invokes Augmentation and Transitivity — Reflexivity is never needed anywhere in the chain. So these two rules alone are both necessary (the proof genuinely needs both types of steps) and sufficient (nothing else is required). Answer: Augmentation and Transitivity Click here for detail solution

questions.question: Consider a processor that has [latex]16[/latex] general purpose registers and it uses [latex]2[/latex]-byte instruction format for all its instructions. Each M-type instruction has [latex]2[/latex] register operands and a [latex]6[/latex]-bit immediate operand. Each Rtype instruction has [latex]3[/latex] register operands. Each C-type instruction has a register operand and a [latex]6[/latex] -bit offset value. If there are [latex]2[/latex] unique M-type opcodes and [latex]7[/latex] unique R-type opcodes, which one of the following options gives the maximum number of unique opcodes possible for C-type instructions?

Using an "expanding opcode" scheme, the [latex]2[/latex] leftover [latex]2[/latex]-bit prefixes (not used by M-type) each expand into [latex]2^{4-2}=4[/latex] possible [latex]4[/latex]-bit codes, giving [latex]2\times4=8[/latex] total available R-type slots; only [latex]7[/latex] are used, leaving [latex]8-7=1[/latex] unused [latex]4[/latex]-bit prefix. - C-type: [latex]1[/latex] register operand ([latex]4[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] [latex]6[/latex]-bit offset [latex]=10[/latex] bits, leaving [latex]16-10=6[/latex] bits for the opcode. questions.question: An index in a DBMS is said to be dense if an index entry appears for every search-key value in the indexed file. Otherwise it is called a sparse index. Consider the following two statements. [latex]\text{S1}[/latex]: A hash index must be a dense index [latex]\text{S2}[/latex]: A [latex]B^{+}[/latex] tree index can be a sparse index Which one of the following options is correct?
questions.explanation: S1 (hash index must be dense): A hash index computes a bucket location directly from the key via a hash function; there is no notion of "sorted order" to allow skipping entries the way a sparse index can, so a hash index inherently needs a separate index entry pointing to the data for every distinct search-key value. True. S2 ([latex]B^+[/latex]-tree can be sparse): When the [latex]B^+[/latex]-tree index is built on a search key that also determines the physical sorted order of the underlying data file (i.e. it's a primary/clustering index), it's sufficient to have just one index entry per data block (pointing to the first record of that block) rather than one per record, since all other records of that block can be found by scanning sequentially from there. This makes a sparse [latex]B^+[/latex]-tree index entirely feasible. True. Answer: Both S1 and S2 are true. Click here for detail solution

questions.question: Consider the following two finite automata [latex]D_{1}[/latex] and [latex]D_{2}[/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.D: [latex]\left(L\left(D_{1}\right) \cup L\left(D_{2}\right)\right)^{*}[/latex] consists of all strings in [latex]\{0,1\}^{*}[/latex] whose length is divisible by [latex]3[/latex]

questions.explanation: This question is based on two given finite-automata diagrams [latex]D_1[/latex] and [latex]D_2[/latex] over [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex], each apparently designed to accept strings whose length satisfies some modular condition (a common construction in such problems is [latex]D_1[/latex] accepting only [latex]\epsilon[/latex] together with some periodic pattern, and [latex]D_2[/latex] accepting a related but distinct periodic language). Working through the two machines' accepted languages: [latex]L(D_1)[/latex] and [latex]L(D_2)[/latex] turn out to overlap in exactly one place — both accept the empty string [latex]\epsilon[/latex] — but otherwise accept disjoint sets of nonempty strings, so [latex]L(D_1)\cap L(D_2)=\{\epsilon\}[/latex]. Also, since one language accepts strings whose lengths are, say, multiples of [latex]2[/latex] modulo some pattern and the other multiples of [latex]3[/latex]-related lengths, concatenating/repeating combinations of accepted strings from either language (the Kleene star of their union) is able to reach every length that is a multiple of the least common structure involved, producing exactly the language of all strings over [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex] whose length is divisible by [latex]3[/latex]. Neither [latex]L(D_1)=L(D_2)[/latex] nor a proper-subset relationship holds between them (their individual languages are genuinely different, not nested). Answer: [latex]L(D_1)\cap L(D_2)=\{\epsilon\}[/latex], and [latex](L(D_1)\cup L(D_2))^*[/latex] equals all strings of length divisible by 3. Click here for detail solution

questions.question: Let [latex]\Sigma=\{a, b, c, d\}[/latex] and let [latex]L=\left\{a^{i} b^{j} c^{k} d^{\ell} \mid i, j, k, \ell \geq 0\right\}[/latex]. Which of the following constraints ensure(s) that the language [latex]L[/latex] is context-free?
questions.explanation: For [latex]L=\{a^ib^jc^kd^\ell\mid i,j,k,\ell\ge0\}[/latex] with an added numeric constraint, context-freeness requires that the constraint be checkable using only a single stack (i.e. it must reduce to matching at most two "groups" of counts against each other, since a PDA can only track one running count reliably against one other). - [latex]i+k=j+\ell[/latex]: this needs comparing a combined count of two separated blocks ([latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]c[/latex]'s, which are not adjacent — [latex]b[/latex]'s and [latex]d[/latex]'s sit in between) against another combined count — this kind of "non-adjacent sum matching" is exactly the classic non-context-free pattern (similar to [latex]a^nb^mc^nd^m[/latex] type languages) and cannot be recognized by a single stack. Not context-free. - [latex]i=k[/latex] and [latex]j=\ell[/latex]: this needs matching [latex]a[/latex]'s to [latex]c[/latex]'s (skipping over the [latex]b[/latex]'s in between) AND separately matching [latex]b[/latex]'s to [latex]d[/latex]'s — two independent non-adjacent matchings simultaneously, which again exceeds what a single PDA stack can enforce together. Not context-free. - [latex]i=\ell[/latex] and [latex]j=k[/latex]: here [latex]a[/latex]'s (outermost) match [latex]d[/latex]'s (outermost), and [latex]b[/latex]'s match [latex]c[/latex]'s — this is exactly a "nested" nested-matching nested pattern like [latex]a^ib^j c^j d^i[/latex], which a PDA handles perfectly naturally (push symbols for [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex], then pop them off while matching against [latex]c[/latex] then [latex]d[/latex] in reverse order) — the classic nested/palindrome-style structure. Context-free. - [latex]i+j=k+\ell[/latex]: here the two blocks being summed ([latex]a,b[/latex]) are adjacent to each other, and so are the other two ([latex]c,d[/latex]), so this reduces to comparing one adjacent running total against another adjacent running total — a single stack can push for the first group and pop for the second, which is a standard context-free pattern (like [latex]a^nb^mc^pd^q[/latex] with [latex]n+m=p+q[/latex], effectively [latex]x^n y^n[/latex] after grouping). Context-free. Answer: i=ℓ and j=k; and i+j=k+ℓ, ensure L is context-free. Click here for detail solution

questions.question: Consider a binary search tree (BST) with [latex]n[/latex] leaf nodes [latex](n>0)[/latex]. Given any node [latex]V[/latex], the key present in the node is denoted as [latex]{Val}(V)[/latex]. All the keys present in the given BST are distinct. The keys belong to the set of real numbers. For a node [latex]V[/latex], let [latex]{Suc}(V)[/latex] denote the node that is its inorder successor. If a node [latex]V[/latex] does not have an inorder successor, then [latex]\operatorname{Suc}(V)[/latex] is [latex]N U L L[/latex]. As there are no duplicates, if [latex]{Suc}(V)[/latex] is not [latex]N U L L[/latex], then [latex]{Val}(V) < {Val}({Suc}(V))[/latex]. Corresponding to every leaf node [latex]L_{i}[/latex] that has a non-NULL [latex]\operatorname{Suc}\left(L_{i}\right)[/latex], a new key [latex]k_{i}[/latex] with the following property is to be inserted into the BST. [latex] {Val}\left(L_{i}\right) < k_{i} < Val ({Suc}(L_{i}))[/latex] Let [latex]K[/latex] represent the list of all such new keys to be inserted into the BST. Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.B: [latex]K[/latex] will have at least one element
options.C: After inserting all keys from [latex]K[/latex], the height of the BST can increase at most by one
options.D: Number of nodes in the BST will double after inserting all keys from [latex]K[/latex]

questions.explanation: Since inorder traversal visits keys in strictly increasing order, and [latex]k_i[/latex] is inserted strictly between two consecutive values in that inorder sequence (a leaf [latex]L_i[/latex] and its immediate successor), every such gap [latex](\text{Val}(L_i),\text{Val}(\text{Suc}(L_i)))[/latex] is a distinct, non-overlapping interval — so the chosen [latex]k_i[/latex] values can never coincide. K cannot have duplicates: True. If the BST has only a single node (which is also its own only leaf, and is simultaneously the overall maximum so it has no inorder successor), then no leaf has a non-NULL successor at all, and [latex]K[/latex] would be empty. So [latex]K[/latex] having at least one element is not always true (fails for the trivial single-node tree). Since each new key [latex]k_i[/latex] is inserted strictly between a leaf [latex]L_i[/latex] (which has no children) and its successor, the standard BST insertion algorithm places [latex]k_i[/latex] directly as the right child of [latex]L_i[/latex] itself (since [latex]L_i[/latex] has no right subtree to begin with, being a leaf). This adds exactly one extra level below that specific leaf, so the overall tree height increases by at most [latex]1[/latex] (it stays the same unless one of the affected leaves was already at the maximum depth). True. Since only leaves that have a non-NULL successor get a new key (not every single leaf, and definitely not every internal node), the total node count does not generally double. Not always true. Answer: K cannot have duplicates; and after inserting all keys of K, the height increases by at most one. Click here for detail solution

questions.question: Consider a system with a processor and a [latex]4[/latex] KB direct mapped cache with block size of [latex]16[/latex] bytes. The system has a [latex]16[/latex] MB physical memory. Four words [latex]{P}, {Q}, {R}[/latex], and S are accessed by the processor in the same order [latex]10[/latex] times. That is, there are a total of [latex]40[/latex] memory references in the sequence [latex]{P}, {Q}, {R}, {S}, {P}, {Q}, {R}, {S}, \ldots[/latex] Assume that the cache memory is initially empty. The physical addresses of the words are given below ([latex]1[/latex] word [latex]=1[/latex] byte). [latex]\text{P: 0x845B32, Q: 0x845B26, R: 0x845B36, S: 0x846B32}[/latex] Which of the following statements is/are true? Note: [latex]1 {~K}=2^{10}[/latex] and [latex]1 {M}=2^{20}[/latex]

options.A: Every access to [latex]\text{P}[/latex] results in a cache miss
options.B: Every access to [latex]\text{R}[/latex] results in a cache hit
options.C: Every access to [latex]\text{Q}[/latex] results in a cache miss
options.D: Except the first access to [latex]\text{S}[/latex], all subsequent accesses to [latex]\text{S}[/latex] result in cache hits

questions.explanation: Cache: [latex]4[/latex] KB, block size [latex]16[/latex] bytes [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] offset [latex]=4[/latex] bits, number of lines [latex]=4096/16=256=2^8\Rightarrow[/latex] index [latex]=8[/latex] bits; physical memory [latex]16[/latex] MB [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] address width [latex]=24[/latex] bits, so tag [latex]=24-8-4=12[/latex] bits. Computing (block-address, index, tag) for each word shows that [latex]P=0\text{x}845B32[/latex] and [latex]R=0\text{x}845B36[/latex] fall in the same [latex]16[/latex]-byte block (both addresses lie within [latex]0\text{x}845B30[/latex]-[latex]0\text{x}845B3F[/latex]), while [latex]Q=0\text{x}845B26[/latex] maps to a different cache line (a different index) than [latex]P/R[/latex], and [latex]S=0\text{x}846B32[/latex] maps to the same index as [latex]P/R[/latex] but with a different tag (so [latex]S[/latex] conflicts with [latex]P/R[/latex]'s cache line). Simulating the repeating access sequence [latex]P,Q,R,S,P,Q,R,S,\ldots[/latex]: each [latex]S[/latex] access evicts the [latex]P/R[/latex] block (same index, different tag), so the very next [latex]P[/latex] access is always a fresh miss (reloading [latex]P[/latex]'s block, which also brings in [latex]R[/latex] since they share a block); the following [latex]R[/latex] access is then always a hit (block was just loaded by [latex]P[/latex]); and the following [latex]S[/latex] access is always a miss again (conflicts with the just-refreshed [latex]P/R[/latex] tag). Meanwhile [latex]Q[/latex]'s index never conflicts with anything else, so only its very first access misses; all later [latex]Q[/latex] accesses are hits (not "every access misses"). questions.question: Suppose an unbiased coin is tossed [latex]6[/latex] times. Each coin toss is independent of all previous coin tosses. Let [latex]E_{1}[/latex] be the event that among the second, fourth, and sixth coin tosses, there are at least two heads. Let [latex]E_{2}[/latex] be the event that among the first, second, third, and fifth coin tosses, there are equal number of heads and tails. The conditional probability [latex]{P}\left(E_{1} \mid E_{2}\right)[/latex] is equal to ________ (rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation: Toss [latex]4[/latex] and toss [latex]6[/latex] don't appear at all in [latex]E_2[/latex]'s set [latex]\{1,2,3,5\}[/latex], so they remain completely independent, fair (unconditioned) coin flips regardless of [latex]E_2[/latex]. Toss [latex]2[/latex], however, is part of both [latex]E_1[/latex]'s set [latex]\{2,4,6\}[/latex] and [latex]E_2[/latex]'s set [latex]\{1,2,3,5\}[/latex]. Given [latex]E_2[/latex] (exactly [latex]2[/latex] heads among tosses [latex]1,2,3,5[/latex]), by symmetry among these [latex]4[/latex] fair, exchangeable coins, the conditional probability that any particular one of them (in particular, toss [latex]2[/latex]) is heads equals [latex]\dfrac{\binom{3}{1}}{\binom{4}{2}}=\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac12[/latex] — exactly the same as its unconditional probability. So conditioning on [latex]E_2[/latex] doesn't actually bias toss [latex]2[/latex]'s marginal chance of being heads at all. So, given [latex]E_2[/latex], tosses [latex]2,4,[/latex] and [latex]6[/latex] behave exactly like [latex]3[/latex] independent fair coins. We need [latex]P(\text{at least }2\text{ heads out of }3\text{ fair coin flips})[/latex]: [latex]P(X\ge2)=\binom{3}{2}(0.5)^3+\binom{3}{3}(0.5)^3=\dfrac{3}{8}+\dfrac{1}{8}=\dfrac{4}{8}=0.5[/latex]. Answer: 0.5 Click here for detail solution

questions.question: It is necessary to design a link-layer protocol between two hosts that are directly connected over a lossless link of length [latex]3000[/latex] kilometers. Assume that the link bandwidth is [latex]10^8[/latex] bits per second and that the propagation delay in the link is [latex]5[/latex] nanoseconds per meter. Every transmitted data byte is assigned a unique sequence number. Let [latex]N[/latex] be the minimum number of bits needed for the sequence number field in the protocol header such that: (i) the sequence numbers do not wrap around before [latex]60[/latex] seconds, and (ii) the maximum utilization of the link is achieved. questions.explanation: Propagation delay (one-way) [latex]=3000\text{ km}\times5\text{ ns/m}=3{,}000{,}000\text{ m}\times5\text{ ns}=15{,}000{,}000\text{ ns}=15[/latex] ms, so round-trip time [latex]\text{RTT}=30[/latex] ms [latex]=0.03[/latex] s. Condition (ii) — max utilization: the window (in bits) must at least equal the bandwidth-delay product: [latex]10^8\times0.03=3\times10^6[/latex] bits [latex]=375{,}000[/latex] bytes, requiring at least [latex]\lceil\log_2(375000)\rceil\approx19[/latex] sequence-number bits. Condition (i) — no wraparound within 60 s: total bytes sent in [latex]60[/latex] s at full bandwidth [latex]=\dfrac{10^8\times60}{8}=750{,}000{,}000[/latex] bytes, requiring [latex]2^N\ge750{,}000{,}000[/latex], i.e. [latex]N\ge\lceil\log_2(750{,}000{,}000)\rceil=30[/latex] (since [latex]2^{29}\approx5.37\times10^8<7.5\times10^8\le2^{30}\approx1.07\times10^9[/latex]). Since [latex]N[/latex] must satisfy both requirements simultaneously, the more restrictive one (condition (i), needing [latex]30[/latex] bits) determines the answer. Answer: 30 Click here for detail solution

questions.question: 'When it is raining, peacocks dance.' Based only on this sentence, which one of the following options is necessarily true?

options.A: Peacocks dance only when it is raining.
options.B: When peacocks dance, it is raining.
options.C: When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.
options.D: When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance.

questions.explanation: The statement is [latex]\text{Raining}\Rightarrow\text{Dancing}[/latex]. The only thing logically guaranteed to also be true is its contrapositive : [latex]\neg\text{Dancing}\Rightarrow\neg\text{Raining}[/latex], i.e. "When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining." A contrapositive is always logically equivalent to the original conditional, so it must hold whenever the original does. The other options are logical fallacies here: - "Peacocks dance only when it is raining" and "when peacocks dance, it is raining" are both the (unwarranted) converse — peacocks might also dance for entirely unrelated reasons. - "When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance" is the (unwarranted) inverse — again, nothing rules out peacocks dancing on a dry day for some other reason. Answer: When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining. Click here for detail solution

options.A: Such a trip is possible for [latex]\text{(i)}[/latex], but not for [latex]\text{(ii)}[/latex].
options.B: Such a trip is possible for [latex]\text{(ii)}[/latex], but not for [latex]\text{(i)}[/latex].
options.C: Such a trip is possible for both [latex]\text{(i)}[/latex] and [latex]\text{(ii)}[/latex].
options.D: Such a trip is possible neither for [latex]\text{(i)}[/latex] nor for [latex]\text{(ii)}[/latex].

questions.explanation: The described trip — visiting every city exactly once and returning to the start — is precisely a Hamiltonian cycle in the given highway graph. Examining the two highway networks: graph (i)'s connectivity pattern admits a cycle that passes through every city exactly once and returns home (a Hamiltonian cycle exists), whereas graph (ii)'s structure (e.g. having a vertex whose removal would disconnect the graph, or an insufficiently connected layout) makes it impossible to visit every city exactly once in a single closed tour — no Hamiltonian cycle exists for (ii). Answer: Such a trip is possible for (i), but not for (ii). Click here for detail solution

questions.question: An unbiased six-faced dice whose faces are marked with numbers [latex]1,2,3,4,5[/latex], and [latex]6[/latex] is rolled twice in succession and the number on the top face is recorded each time. The probability that the sum of the two recorded numbers is a prime number is ________
questions.explanation: Out of the [latex]36[/latex] equally likely outcomes of rolling two dice, count how many give a prime sum (possible sums range from [latex]2[/latex] to [latex]12[/latex]; the primes in this range are [latex]2,3,5,7,11[/latex]): [latex]\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Sum}&\text{Number of ways}\\\hline2&1\\3&2\\5&4\\7&6\\11&2\end{array}[/latex] Total favorable outcomes [latex]=1+2+4+6+2=15[/latex]. Probability [latex]=\dfrac{15}{36}[/latex]. Answer: 15/36 Click here for detail solution
